subject: Computer Networking
title: DNSSEC: Trusting DNS Answers
description: A fast breakdown of DNSSEC: Trusting DNS Answers for builders.

hook.text: You ask DNS for a bank's IP. What if someone poisons the answer and sends you to a fake site?

buildup.text: DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records. Your resolver can verify that the answer is authentic.

discovery.text: Signatures chain from the root zone down. Each level vouches for the next, building a chain of trust.

twist.text: DNSSEC doesn't encrypt queries — it only proves answers are genuine. Privacy needs DNS-over-HTTPS separately.

climax.text: Adoption is slow because it adds complexity and can break misconfigured domains. But it prevents cache poisoning.

punchline.text: DNSSEC proves the answer came from the right source.

quiz.question: What does DNSSEC protect against?
options: Forged DNS answers and cache poisoning

details.summary: DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records, allowing resolvers to verify that responses are authentic and have not been tampered with. Each zone signs its records with a private key, and parent zones vouch for child zones through a chain of trust anchored at the DNS root.
details.whyItMatters: Without DNSSEC, attackers can forge DNS responses to redirect users to malicious sites. DNSSEC prevents cache poisoning and ensures DNS answers genuinely come from the authorized source.
takeaways: DNSSEC signs DNS records with cryptographic signatures
A chain of trust from the root verifies signature authenticity
Resolvers reject responses that fail signature validation

faq.question: How does DNSSEC prevent DNS spoofing?
faq.answer: Every DNS zone signs its records with a private key. Resolvers verify signatures using the corresponding public key, which is authenticated through a chain of trust to the DNS root. Forged or tampered responses fail verification and are discarded, preventing attackers from redirecting users.

faq.question: Why is DNSSEC not universally deployed?
faq.answer: DNSSEC adds complexity to DNS management, increases response sizes, and requires careful key rotation. Misconfigured DNSSEC causes domain outages because resolvers reject unsigned or incorrectly signed responses. Many domain operators find the operational risk outweighs the security benefit.
